Surat al-Muzzammil has twenty-seven verses and is Meccan, all of it according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata' and Jabir. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except two verses of it, ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10] and the one after it. This was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Tha'labi said: the words of God, ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], through to the end of the surah, were revealed at Medina.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who wraps himself [in garments]! Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in a measured recitation.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1–4]

In this passage there are eight issues.

The first: God's words, ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾. Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: al-Muzzammil is originally al-mutazammil, so the ta' was assimilated into the za'. The same applies to al-Muddaththir. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited it according to the original form, al-mutazammil and al-mutaddathir. Sa'id [recited] al-muzzammil.[[Perhaps this is what some exegetes meant by their saying: some of the early generation read (al-muzzammil) with a fatha on the za' and its lightening, and a fatha on the mim with its doubling.]] As for the root of al-muzzammil, there are two views. The first is that it means "the one who bears a burden," from zamala al-shay' meaning he carried it, and from this comes al-zamilah (the baggage camel), because it carries household goods.[[al-qumash: the poorer household goods, also called saqt al-mata'.]] The second is that al-muzzammil means "the one who is wrapped up," as one says tazammala and tadaththara bi-thawbihi when he covers himself with his garment, and zammala ghayrahu when he covers someone else. Anything wrapped is said to be zummila and duththira. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Great among folk, in a rough cloak, wrapped up"[[First half of the line: "As if our father, among the twists of its rain..."]]

The second: God's words, ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾, are addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and concerning this there are three views. The first is the saying of Ikrimah: "O you who wraps himself" means "clothed with prophethood and bound to the message." It is also related from him: "O you who has been burdened with this matter," that is, he carried it and then slackened. He used to recite (al-muzammal) with a lightened za' and a fatha on the mim with its doubling, on the basis that the object is elided; likewise (al-muddaththar). The meaning is "the one who wraps himself," and "the one who wraps himself," or "the one whom another has wrapped." The second: "O you who wraps himself in the Qur'an," said by Ibn Abbas. The third: "al-muzzammil with his garments," said by Qatadah and others. Al-Nakha'i said: he was wrapped in a velvet cloak. Aisha said: [he was wrapped] in a mirt (a wrap) fourteen cubits long, half of it over me while I slept and half over the Prophet (ﷺ) while he prayed. By God, it was neither silk nor brocade, nor mir'iza' (the soft down beneath the goat's hair), nor shining silk, nor wool; its warp was hair and its weft was fleece. This was related by al-Tha'labi. I say: this statement from Aisha indicates that the surah is Medinan, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consummate marriage with her except at Medina. What is mentioned about its being Meccan is not sound. And God knows best. Al-Dahhak said: he wrapped himself in his garments for sleep. It has also been said: word reached him from the polytheists of an evil saying about him, and it grieved him, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1] and ﴿O you who covers himself﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1]. It has also been said that this was at the beginning of what was revealed to him. When he heard the words of the angel and looked at him, trembling seized him, and he went to his family and said: "Wrap me, cover me" (zammiluni, daththiruni). Its meaning is related from Ibn Abbas. The wise men said: he was addressed as al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir at the beginning of the matter, because at that time he had not yet borne anything of the conveying of the message. Ibn al-Arabi said: the interpretation of ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ has been disputed. Some took it literally, saying: "O you who has wrapped himself in his garment or his velvet cloak, arise," as said by Ibrahim and Qatadah. Others took it figuratively, as if it were said to him: "O you who has clothed himself with prophethood," as said by Ikrimah. This interpretation would only be valid if the mim were fatha-ed and doubled in the passive form, the object being unnamed; but in the active form, as it is in the text, it is invalid. I say: we have already shown that it is by elision of the object, and it has been recited thus, so its meaning is sound. He said: as for those who say that he was burdened with the Qur'an, that is correct in the figurative sense, but we have already mentioned that it is not needed.

The third: al-Suhayli said: al-Muzzammil is not one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ), nor was he known by it, as some people have claimed, counting it among his names, peace be upon him. Rather, al-Muzzammil is a name derived from his state at the time of the address, and likewise al-Muddaththir. In addressing him by this name there are two benefits. The first is gentleness, for when the Arabs intend to be gentle with the one addressed and to avoid reproach, they call him by a name derived from the state he is in. Such is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ali, when he was angry with Fatimah (may God be pleased with them both): he came to him while he was sleeping and dust had stuck to his side, and he said to him: "Get up, O father of dust" (qum ya aba turab), to signal that he was not blaming him and to be gentle with him. Likewise the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, to Hudhayfah: "Get up, O sleeper" (qum ya nawman), when he was asleep, as gentleness and as a signal of leaving off blame and reproach.[[In a, h, l: (al-ta'nis, "familiarity").]] So God's saying to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿O you who wraps himself, stand﴾, contains familiarity and gentleness, so that he would perceive that he was not being blamed. The second benefit is an alert to every sleeper wrapped up for the night, so that he awakens to standing in prayer by night and to the remembrance of God in it, because a name derived from an action is shared with the addressee by everyone who does that deed and has that attribute.

The fourth: God's words, ﴿Stand through the night﴾. The common recitation is with a kasra on the mim, because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Abu al-Sammal recited it with a damma on the mim, following the damma of the qaf. And a fatha was reported, for its lightness. Uthman ibn Jinni said: the purpose of this vowel is to articulate, so as to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters; whichever vowel is used, the purpose is achieved. It is one of the intransitive verbs that do not take a direct object. As for a time or place adverb, it is permissible with it; but a place adverb is not reached except through a preposition. You do not say qumtu al-dar (I stood the house), until you say qumtu wasta al-dar (I stood in the middle of the house) or kharija al-dar (outside the house). It has been said that qum here means pray; it was expressed by it and borrowed for it, until it became customary through frequency of use.

The fifth: al-layl (the night) is the limit of the night, from the sunset to the break of dawn. Its explanation has already been given in the surah al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 2, p. 192.]] It has been disputed whether his standing was an obligation and a binding duty, or a recommendation and encouragement. The evidence strengthens that his standing was binding and obligatory, because recommendation and encouragement do not apply to part of the night rather than another part, since standing is not restricted to one time rather than another. Also, a specific time was given for it, from Aisha and others, as will come. It has also been disputed whether it was obligatory for the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, or for him and for those prophets before him, or for him and for his community. There are three views. The first is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, because the address was directed to him specifically. The second is the saying of Ibn Abbas, who said: standing in the night was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and upon the prophets before him. The third is the saying of Aisha and also of Ibn Abbas, and it is the sound one, as in Sahih Muslim from Zurarah ibn Awfa that Sa'd ibn Hisham ibn Amir wanted to go out to fight in the way of God... the hadith, in which: I said to Aisha: "Tell me about the standing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" She said: "Do you not recite: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, made standing in the night obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions stood for a year, while God, Mighty and Majestic, held back its conclusion for twelve months in the heavens, until God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed at the end of this surah the lightening, so the standing in the night became a voluntary act after an obligation." And he mentioned the hadith. Waki' and Ya'la reported, saying: Mis'ar related to us from Simak al-Hanafi who said: I heard Ibn Abbas say: "When the beginning of ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ was revealed, they used to stand approximately as they stand in the month of Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and between its beginning and its end was about a year." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions remained for ten years standing through the night, then after ten years was revealed: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], so God lightened it for them.

The sixth: God's words, ﴿except a little﴾, are an exception from the night. That is: pray the whole night except a small part of it, because standing for all of it continuously is not possible, so He excepted a little of it for the rest of the body. The "little" of a thing is what is less than half. It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: "The little is less than a tenth and a sixth." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: a third. Then He said: ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little﴾. That was a lightening, since the time of standing was not fixed, so people stood until their feet swelled. Then this was abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) by His saying: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Al-Akhfash said: "half of it" means "or half of it," as one says: give him one dirham, two dirhams, three; he means: or two dirhams, or three. Al-Zajjaj said: "half of it" is a substitution for "the night," and "except a little" is an exception from "the half." The pronoun in "from it" and "over it" refers to the half. The meaning: stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little, to a third, or add to it a little, to two-thirds; as if He said: stand two-thirds of the night, or its half, or its third. It has been said that "half of it" is a substitution for His saying "a little," and he was given the choice between three: between standing for the whole half, and between reducing from it, and between standing for more than it. The sense of the speech is as if: "Stand the night except its half, or less than its half, or more than its half." In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, descends to the lowest heaven every night when the first third of the night has passed, and says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there who calls upon Me that I may answer him? Who is there who asks of Me that I may give him? Who is there who seeks forgiveness of Me that I may forgive him?' He continues thus until the dawn breaks." A similar report from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id both, and it indicates the encouragement of standing for two-thirds of the night. In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When half of the night has passed, or its two-thirds, God descends..." the hadith. He related it through two routes from Abu Hurayrah in this form, with doubt. In the book of al-Nasa'i it has come from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, may God be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, waits until the first half of the night has passed, then He commands a caller who says: 'Is there any supplicant who will be answered? Is there any seeker of forgiveness who will be forgiven? Is there any petitioner who will be given?'" Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it. This hadith, together with its soundness, clarifies the meaning of descent, and that it occurs at the middle of the night. Ibn Majah related from the hadith of Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salamah and Abu Abd Allah al-Aghar, from Abu Hurayrah:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, descends every night when the last third of the night remains, and He says: 'Who will ask Me, that I may give to him? Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will seek forgiveness from Me, that I may forgive him?' until dawn breaks." So they would prefer to pray the last part of the night over the first part. Our scholars said: "With this order the hadith and the Qur'an are harmonized, for both derive their light from one niche."

In al-Muwatta' (the collection of Imam Malik) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah. When half the night had passed, or a little before or a little after, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up, went to a hanging waterskin, and performed a light ablution." And he mentioned the hadith.

The seventh issue: The scholars differed concerning what abrogated (naskh, abrogation) the command to perform the night prayer. From Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha: the abrogating verse is His saying, "Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night," to the end of the surah (al-Muzzammil 20). It was also said that it is His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" (al-Muzzammil 20). From Ibn 'Abbas also: it was abrogated by His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" (al-Muzzammil 20). From 'A'isha too, and from al-Shafi'i, Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan: it was abrogated by the five daily prayers. It was also said that the abrogating verse is His saying, "So recite what is easy of it" (al-Muzzammil 20). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: "When the verse 'O you wrapped in garments' was revealed, they stood (in prayer) until their feet and calves swelled. Then the verse 'So recite what is easy of it' was revealed." Some scholars said: "This was an obligation that was abrogated by another obligation, which was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) because of his excellence, as Allah says: 'And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you' (al-Isra' 79)."

I say: The first opinion encompasses all of these views, and Allah says: "And establish the prayer" (al-Muzzammil 20), so the saying of those who said that the abrogating ruling is the five prayers is included in it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin held that the night prayer is an obligation upon every Muslim, even if it is only as much as the time it takes to milk a sheep. It is also reported from al-Hasan that he said, concerning this verse, "Praise be to Allah" is a voluntary act after the obligatory prayer. This is the correct view, Allah willing, because of what has come in the Qur'an and the Sunnah regarding its merit and the encouragement to perform it.

From 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "I used to place a mat for the Prophet (ﷺ) on which he would pray during the night. The people heard about it, and when he saw their numbers he disliked that, and feared that the night prayer would be prescribed for them. So he entered the house as one who was angry. They began to clear their throats and spit, and he came out to them and said: 'O people, take on the deeds that you are able to perform, for Allah does not tire of rewarding you until you tire of working. The best deed is the most consistent of it, even if it is small.'" Then the verse "O you wrapped in garments" was revealed, and it was made obligatory upon them and treated as an obligation, to the extent that one of them would tie a rope and hold onto it. They continued this for eight months. Then Allah had mercy on them and revealed: "Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night" (al-Muzzammil 20), and He returned them to the obligatory prayers and lifted from them the night prayer, except what they performed voluntarily.

I say: This hadith of 'A'isha was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, and its meaning is established in the Sahih up to her words "even if it is small." The rest of it indicates that the verse "O you wrapped in garments" was revealed in Medina, and that they continued praying for eight months. It has previously been mentioned from her in Sahih Muslim that it was a full year. Al-Mawardi related from her a third opinion, that it was sixteen months, and he mentioned no other from her. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the period between the beginning of al-Muzzammil and its end was one year. He said: "As for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it was obligatory upon him." In one report from him there are two views: one, that it remained obligatory upon him until Allah took him; the second, that it was abrogated for him just as it was abrogated for his community. Regarding the period of its obligation until it was abrogated there are two views: one, that it is the period set for his community in the two previous opinions, namely Ibn 'Abbas's saying "a year" and 'A'isha's saying "sixteen months." The second: that it was ten years, until it was lightened for him through abrogation, an increase in the obligation so that he would be distinguished by the performance of the message. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. I say: This contradicts what al-Tha'labi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as mentioned earlier, so consider it carefully. Further explanation of this issue will come at the end of the surah, Allah willing.

The eighth issue: His saying, "And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation" (al-Muzzammil 4), meaning: do not hasten in reciting the Qur'an, but recite it slowly and clearly, reflecting on its meanings. Al-Dahhak said: "Recite it letter by letter." Mujahid said: "The people most beloved to Allah in recitation are those who understand it best." Tartil means arranging, ordering, and good arrangement. From it comes the phrase "a thaghr ratal" and "ratal," with the 'ayn vowelled with a kasra or a fatha, meaning when the teeth are well arranged. Its explanation has already been given in the introduction of this book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 17.]

It is narrated by al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a man who was reciting a verse and weeping, and he said: "Did you not hear the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation'? This is tartil." 'Alqama heard a man reciting beautifully and said: "He has indeed recited the Qur'an in measured manner; may my father and mother be ransomed for him." Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: "Reflect upon the subtleties of His address, compel yourself to act upon its rulings, your heart to understand its meanings, and your inner self to turn towards it."

'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the Qur'an reciter will be brought, and he will be made to stand at the first step of Paradise, and it will be said to him: 'Recite, ascend, and recite in measured manner as you used to recite in the world, for your station will be at the last verse you recite.'" Abu Dawud recorded it, and it has been mentioned previously at the beginning of the book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 8.]

Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to prolong his voice in recitation, stretching the vowels.

The first is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, because the address was directed to him specifically. The second is the saying of Ibn Abbas, who said: standing in the night was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and upon the prophets before him. She said: "Do you not recite: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, made standing in the night obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions stood for a year, while God, Mighty and Majestic, held back its conclusion for twelve months in the heavens, until God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed at the end of this surah the lightening, so the standing in the night became a voluntary act after an obligation." And he mentioned the hadith. Waki' and Ya'la reported, saying: Mis'ar related to us from Simak al-Hanafi who said: I heard Ibn Abbas say: "When the beginning of ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ was revealed, they used to stand approximately as they stand in the month of Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and between its beginning and its end was about a year." The sixth: God's words, ﴿except a little﴾, are an exception from the night. That is: pray the whole night except a small part of it, because standing for all of it continuously is not possible, so He excepted a little of it for the rest of the body. Then He said: ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little﴾. That was a lightening, since the time of standing was not fixed, so people stood until their feet swelled. Then this was abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) by His saying: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Al-Zajjaj said: "half of it" is a substitution for "the night," and "except a little" is an exception from "the half." The pronoun in "from it" and "over it" refers to the half. The meaning: stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little, to a third, or add to it a little, to two-thirds; as if He said: stand two-thirds of the night, or its half, or its third. It has been said that "half of it" is a substitution for His saying "a little," and he was given the choice between three: between standing for the whole half, and between reducing from it, and between standing for more than it. The sense of the speech is as if: "Stand the night except its half, or less than its half, or more than its half." In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, descends to the lowest heaven every night when the first third of the night has passed, and says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there who calls upon Me that I may answer him? Who is there who asks of Me that I may give him? Who is there who seeks forgiveness of Me that I may forgive him?' He continues thus until the dawn breaks." A similar report from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id both, and it indicates the encouragement of standing for two-thirds of the night. In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When half of the night has passed, or its two-thirds, God descends..." the hadith. He related it through two routes from Abu Hurayrah in this form, with doubt. Ibn Majah related from the hadith of Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salamah and Abu Abd Allah al-Aghar, from Abu Hurayrah:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, descends every night when the last third of the night remains, and He says: 'Who will ask Me, that I may give to him? Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will seek forgiveness from Me, that I may forgive him?' until dawn breaks." So they would prefer to pray the last part of the night over the first part. In al-Muwatta' (the collection of Imam Malik) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah. From Ibn 'Abbas also: it was abrogated by His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" (al-Muzzammil 20). From 'A'isha too, and from al-Shafi'i, Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan: it was abrogated by the five daily prayers. It was also said that the abrogating verse is His saying, "So recite what is easy of it" (al-Muzzammil 20). Regarding the period of its obligation until it was abrogated there are two views: one, that it is the period set for his community in the two previous opinions, namely Ibn 'Abbas's saying "a year" and 'A'isha's saying "sixteen months." Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to prolong his voice in recitation, stretching the vowels.

Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except two verses of it, ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10] and the one after it. This was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Tha'labi said: the words of God, ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], through to the end of the surah, were revealed at Medina.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who wraps himself [in garments]! Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in a measured recitation.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1–4]

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited it according to the original form, al-mutazammil and al-mutaddathir. Sa'id [recited] al-muzzammil.[[Perhaps this is what some exegetes meant by their saying: some of the early generation read (al-muzzammil) with a fatha on the za' and its lightening, and a fatha on the mim with its doubling.]] As for the root of al-muzzammil, there are two views. The first is that it means "the one who bears a burden," from zamala al-shay' meaning he carried it, and from this comes al-zamilah (the baggage camel), because it carries household goods.[[al-qumash: the poorer household goods, also called saqt al-mata'.]] The second is that al-muzzammil means "the one who is wrapped up," as one says tazammala and tadaththara bi-thawbihi when he covers himself with his garment, and zammala ghayrahu when he covers someone else. Anything wrapped is said to be zummila and duththira. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Great among folk, in a rough cloak, wrapped up"[[First half of the line: "As if our father, among the twists of its rain..."]]

The second: God's words, ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾, are addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and concerning this there are three views. The first is the saying of Ikrimah: "O you who wraps himself" means "clothed with prophethood and bound to the message." It is also related from him: "O you who has been burdened with this matter," that is, he carried it and then slackened. He used to recite (al-muzammal) with a lightened za' and a fatha on the mim with its doubling, on the basis that the object is elided; likewise (al-muddaththar). The meaning is "the one who wraps himself," and "the one who wraps himself," or "the one whom another has wrapped." The second: "O you who wraps himself in the Qur'an," said by Ibn Abbas. The third: "al-muzzammil with his garments," said by Qatadah and others. Al-Nakha'i said: he was wrapped in a velvet cloak. Aisha said: [he was wrapped] in a mirt (a wrap) fourteen cubits long, half of it over me while I slept and half over the Prophet (ﷺ) while he prayed. By God, it was neither silk nor brocade, nor mir'iza' (the soft down beneath the goat's hair), nor shining silk, nor wool; its warp was hair and its weft was fleece. This was related by al-Tha'labi. I say: this statement from Aisha indicates that the surah is Medinan, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consummate marriage with her except at Medina. What is mentioned about its being Meccan is not sound. And God knows best. Al-Dahhak said: he wrapped himself in his garments for sleep. It has also been said: word reached him from the polytheists of an evil saying about him, and it grieved him, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1] and ﴿O you who covers himself﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1]. It has also been said that this was at the beginning of what was revealed to him. When he heard the words of the angel and looked at him, trembling seized him, and he went to his family and said: "Wrap me, cover me" (zammiluni, daththiruni). Its meaning is related from Ibn Abbas. The wise men said: he was addressed as al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir at the beginning of the matter, because at that time he had not yet borne anything of the conveying of the message. They continued this for eight months. Then Allah had mercy on them and revealed: "Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night" (al-Muzzammil 20), and He returned them to the obligatory prayers and lifted from them the night prayer, except what they performed voluntarily.

I say: This hadith of 'A'isha was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, and its meaning is established in the Sahih up to her words "even if it is small." The rest of it indicates that the verse "O you wrapped in garments" was revealed in Medina, and that they continued praying for eight months. It has previously been mentioned from her in Sahih Muslim that it was a full year. Al-Mawardi related from her a third opinion, that it was sixteen months, and he mentioned no other from her. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the period between the beginning of al-Muzzammil and its end was one year. He said: "As for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it was obligatory upon him." In one report from him there are two views: one, that it remained obligatory upon him until Allah took him; the second, that it was abrogated for him just as it was abrogated for his community. Regarding the period of its obligation until it was abrogated there are two views: one, that it is the period set for his community in the two previous opinions, namely Ibn 'Abbas's saying "a year" and 'A'isha's saying "sixteen months." The second: that it was ten years, until it was lightened for him through abrogation, an increase in the obligation so that he would be distinguished by the performance of the message. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. I say: This contradicts what al-Tha'labi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as mentioned earlier, so consider it carefully. Further explanation of this issue will come at the end of the surah, Allah willing.

The eighth issue: His saying, "And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation" (al-Muzzammil 4), meaning: do not hasten in reciting the Qur'an, but recite it slowly and clearly, reflecting on its meanings. Al-Dahhak said: "Recite it letter by letter." Mujahid said: "The people most beloved to Allah in recitation are those who understand it best." Tartil means arranging, ordering, and good arrangement. From it comes the phrase "a thaghr ratal" and "ratal," with the 'ayn vowelled with a kasra or a fatha, meaning when the teeth are well arranged. Its explanation has already been given in the introduction of this book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 17.]

It is narrated by al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a man who was reciting a verse and weeping, and he said: "Did you not hear the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation'? This is tartil." 'Alqama heard a man reciting beautifully and said: "He has indeed recited the Qur'an in measured manner; may my father and mother be ransomed for him." Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: "Reflect upon the subtleties of His address, compel yourself to act upon its rulings, your heart to understand its meanings, and your inner self to turn towards it."

'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the Qur'an reciter will be brought, and he will be made to stand at the first step of Paradise, and it will be said to him: 'Recite, ascend, and recite in measured manner as you used to recite in the world, for your station will be at the last verse you recite.'" Abu Dawud recorded it, and it has been mentioned previously at the beginning of the book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 8.]

Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to prolong his voice in recitation, stretching the vowels.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 73, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Muzzammil has twenty-seven verses and is Meccan, all of it according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata' and Jabir. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except two verses of it, ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10] and the one after it. This was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Tha'labi said: the words of God, ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], through to the end of the surah, were revealed at Medina.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who wraps himself [in garments]! Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in a measured recitation.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1–4]

In this passage there are eight issues.

The first: God's words, ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾. Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: al-Muzzammil is originally al-mutazammil, so the ta' was assimilated into the za'. The same applies to al-Muddaththir. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited it according to the original form, al-mutazammil and al-mutaddathir. Sa'id [recited] al-muzzammil.[[Perhaps this is what some exegetes meant by their saying: some of the early generation read (al-muzzammil) with a fatha on the za' and its lightening, and a fatha on the mim with its doubling.]] As for the root of al-muzzammil, there are two views. The first is that it means "the one who bears a burden," from zamala al-shay' meaning he carried it, and from this comes al-zamilah (the baggage camel), because it carries household goods.[[al-qumash: the poorer household goods, also called saqt al-mata'.]] The second is that al-muzzammil means "the one who is wrapped up," as one says tazammala and tadaththara bi-thawbihi when he covers himself with his garment, and zammala ghayrahu when he covers someone else. Anything wrapped is said to be zummila and duththira. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Great among folk, in a rough cloak, wrapped up"[[First half of the line: "As if our father, among the twists of its rain..."]]

The second: God's words, ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾, are addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and concerning this there are three views. The first is the saying of Ikrimah: "O you who wraps himself" means "clothed with prophethood and bound to the message." It is also related from him: "O you who has been burdened with this matter," that is, he carried it and then slackened. He used to recite (al-muzammal) with a lightened za' and a fatha on the mim with its doubling, on the basis that the object is elided; likewise (al-muddaththar). The meaning is "the one who wraps himself," and "the one who wraps himself," or "the one whom another has wrapped." The second: "O you who wraps himself in the Qur'an," said by Ibn Abbas. The third: "al-muzzammil with his garments," said by Qatadah and others. Al-Nakha'i said: he was wrapped in a velvet cloak. Aisha said: [he was wrapped] in a mirt (a wrap) fourteen cubits long, half of it over me while I slept and half over the Prophet (ﷺ) while he prayed. By God, it was neither silk nor brocade, nor mir'iza' (the soft down beneath the goat's hair), nor shining silk, nor wool; its warp was hair and its weft was fleece. This was related by al-Tha'labi. I say: this statement from Aisha indicates that the surah is Medinan, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consummate marriage with her except at Medina. What is mentioned about its being Meccan is not sound. And God knows best. Al-Dahhak said: he wrapped himself in his garments for sleep. It has also been said: word reached him from the polytheists of an evil saying about him, and it grieved him, so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1] and ﴿O you who covers himself﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1]. It has also been said that this was at the beginning of what was revealed to him. When he heard the words of the angel and looked at him, trembling seized him, and he went to his family and said: "Wrap me, cover me" (zammiluni, daththiruni). Its meaning is related from Ibn Abbas. The wise men said: he was addressed as al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir at the beginning of the matter, because at that time he had not yet borne anything of the conveying of the message. Ibn al-Arabi said: the interpretation of ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ has been disputed. Some took it literally, saying: "O you who has wrapped himself in his garment or his velvet cloak, arise," as said by Ibrahim and Qatadah. Others took it figuratively, as if it were said to him: "O you who has clothed himself with prophethood," as said by Ikrimah. This interpretation would only be valid if the mim were fatha-ed and doubled in the passive form, the object being unnamed; but in the active form, as it is in the text, it is invalid. I say: we have already shown that it is by elision of the object, and it has been recited thus, so its meaning is sound. He said: as for those who say that he was burdened with the Qur'an, that is correct in the figurative sense, but we have already mentioned that it is not needed.

The third: al-Suhayli said: al-Muzzammil is not one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ), nor was he known by it, as some people have claimed, counting it among his names, peace be upon him. Rather, al-Muzzammil is a name derived from his state at the time of the address, and likewise al-Muddaththir. In addressing him by this name there are two benefits. The first is gentleness, for when the Arabs intend to be gentle with the one addressed and to avoid reproach, they call him by a name derived from the state he is in. Such is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ali, when he was angry with Fatimah (may God be pleased with them both): he came to him while he was sleeping and dust had stuck to his side, and he said to him: "Get up, O father of dust" (qum ya aba turab), to signal that he was not blaming him and to be gentle with him. Likewise the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, to Hudhayfah: "Get up, O sleeper" (qum ya nawman), when he was asleep, as gentleness and as a signal of leaving off blame and reproach.[[In a, h, l: (al-ta'nis, "familiarity").]] So God's saying to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿O you who wraps himself, stand﴾, contains familiarity and gentleness, so that he would perceive that he was not being blamed. The second benefit is an alert to every sleeper wrapped up for the night, so that he awakens to standing in prayer by night and to the remembrance of God in it, because a name derived from an action is shared with the addressee by everyone who does that deed and has that attribute.

The fourth: God's words, ﴿Stand through the night﴾. The common recitation is with a kasra on the mim, because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Abu al-Sammal recited it with a damma on the mim, following the damma of the qaf. And a fatha was reported, for its lightness. Uthman ibn Jinni said: the purpose of this vowel is to articulate, so as to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters; whichever vowel is used, the purpose is achieved. It is one of the intransitive verbs that do not take a direct object. As for a time or place adverb, it is permissible with it; but a place adverb is not reached except through a preposition. You do not say qumtu al-dar (I stood the house), until you say qumtu wasta al-dar (I stood in the middle of the house) or kharija al-dar (outside the house). It has been said that qum here means pray; it was expressed by it and borrowed for it, until it became customary through frequency of use.

The fifth: al-layl (the night) is the limit of the night, from the sunset to the break of dawn. Its explanation has already been given in the surah al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 2, p. 192.]] It has been disputed whether his standing was an obligation and a binding duty, or a recommendation and encouragement. The evidence strengthens that his standing was binding and obligatory, because recommendation and encouragement do not apply to part of the night rather than another part, since standing is not restricted to one time rather than another. Also, a specific time was given for it, from Aisha and others, as will come. It has also been disputed whether it was obligatory for the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, or for him and for those prophets before him, or for him and for his community. There are three views. The first is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, because the address was directed to him specifically. The second is the saying of Ibn Abbas, who said: standing in the night was obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and upon the prophets before him. The third is the saying of Aisha and also of Ibn Abbas, and it is the sound one, as in Sahih Muslim from Zurarah ibn Awfa that Sa'd ibn Hisham ibn Amir wanted to go out to fight in the way of God... the hadith, in which: I said to Aisha: "Tell me about the standing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" She said: "Do you not recite: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, made standing in the night obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions stood for a year, while God, Mighty and Majestic, held back its conclusion for twelve months in the heavens, until God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed at the end of this surah the lightening, so the standing in the night became a voluntary act after an obligation." And he mentioned the hadith. Waki' and Ya'la reported, saying: Mis'ar related to us from Simak al-Hanafi who said: I heard Ibn Abbas say: "When the beginning of ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ was revealed, they used to stand approximately as they stand in the month of Ramadan, until its end was revealed, and between its beginning and its end was about a year." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions remained for ten years standing through the night, then after ten years was revealed: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], so God lightened it for them.

The sixth: God's words, ﴿except a little﴾, are an exception from the night. That is: pray the whole night except a small part of it, because standing for all of it continuously is not possible, so He excepted a little of it for the rest of the body. The "little" of a thing is what is less than half. It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: "The little is less than a tenth and a sixth." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: a third. Then He said: ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little﴾. That was a lightening, since the time of standing was not fixed, so people stood until their feet swelled. Then this was abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) by His saying: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Al-Akhfash said: "half of it" means "or half of it," as one says: give him one dirham, two dirhams, three; he means: or two dirhams, or three. Al-Zajjaj said: "half of it" is a substitution for "the night," and "except a little" is an exception from "the half." The pronoun in "from it" and "over it" refers to the half. The meaning: stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little, to a third, or add to it a little, to two-thirds; as if He said: stand two-thirds of the night, or its half, or its third. It has been said that "half of it" is a substitution for His saying "a little," and he was given the choice between three: between standing for the whole half, and between reducing from it, and between standing for more than it. The sense of the speech is as if: "Stand the night except its half, or less than its half, or more than its half." In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, descends to the lowest heaven every night when the first third of the night has passed, and says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there who calls upon Me that I may answer him? Who is there who asks of Me that I may give him? Who is there who seeks forgiveness of Me that I may forgive him?' He continues thus until the dawn breaks." A similar report from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id both, and it indicates the encouragement of standing for two-thirds of the night. In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When half of the night has passed, or its two-thirds, God descends..." the hadith. He related it through two routes from Abu Hurayrah in this form, with doubt. In the book of al-Nasa'i it has come from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, may God be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, waits until the first half of the night has passed, then He commands a caller who says: 'Is there any supplicant who will be answered? Is there any seeker of forgiveness who will be forgiven? Is there any petitioner who will be given?'" Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it. This hadith, together with its soundness, clarifies the meaning of descent, and that it occurs at the middle of the night. Ibn Majah related from the hadith of Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salamah and Abu Abd Allah al-Aghar, from Abu Hurayrah:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, descends every night when the last third of the night remains, and He says: 'Who will ask Me, that I may give to him? Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will seek forgiveness from Me, that I may forgive him?' until dawn breaks." So they would prefer to pray the last part of the night over the first part. Our scholars said: "With this order the hadith and the Qur'an are harmonized, for both derive their light from one niche."

In al-Muwatta' (the collection of Imam Malik) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah. When half the night had passed, or a little before or a little after, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up, went to a hanging waterskin, and performed a light ablution." And he mentioned the hadith.

The seventh issue: The scholars differed concerning what abrogated (naskh, abrogation) the command to perform the night prayer. From Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha: the abrogating verse is His saying, "Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night," to the end of the surah (al-Muzzammil 20). It was also said that it is His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" (al-Muzzammil 20). From Ibn 'Abbas also: it was abrogated by His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" (al-Muzzammil 20). From 'A'isha too, and from al-Shafi'i, Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan: it was abrogated by the five daily prayers. It was also said that the abrogating verse is His saying, "So recite what is easy of it" (al-Muzzammil 20). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: "When the verse 'O you wrapped in garments' was revealed, they stood (in prayer) until their feet and calves swelled. Then the verse 'So recite what is easy of it' was revealed." Some scholars said: "This was an obligation that was abrogated by another obligation, which was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) because of his excellence, as Allah says: 'And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you' (al-Isra' 79)."

I say: The first opinion encompasses all of these views, and Allah says: "And establish the prayer" (al-Muzzammil 20), so the saying of those who said that the abrogating ruling is the five prayers is included in it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin held that the night prayer is an obligation upon every Muslim, even if it is only as much as the time it takes to milk a sheep. It is also reported from al-Hasan that he said, concerning this verse, "Praise be to Allah" is a voluntary act after the obligatory prayer. This is the correct view, Allah willing, because of what has come in the Qur'an and the Sunnah regarding its merit and the encouragement to perform it.

From 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "I used to place a mat for the Prophet (ﷺ) on which he would pray during the night. The people heard about it, and when he saw their numbers he disliked that, and feared that the night prayer would be prescribed for them. So he entered the house as one who was angry. They began to clear their throats and spit, and he came out to them and said: 'O people, take on the deeds that you are able to perform, for Allah does not tire of rewarding you until you tire of working. The best deed is the most consistent of it, even if it is small.'" Then the verse "O you wrapped in garments" was revealed, and it was made obligatory upon them and treated as an obligation, to the extent that one of them would tie a rope and hold onto it. They continued this for eight months. Then Allah had mercy on them and revealed: "Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night" (al-Muzzammil 20), and He returned them to the obligatory prayers and lifted from them the night prayer, except what they performed voluntarily.

I say: This hadith of 'A'isha was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, and its meaning is established in the Sahih up to her words "even if it is small." The rest of it indicates that the verse "O you wrapped in garments" was revealed in Medina, and that they continued praying for eight months. It has previously been mentioned from her in Sahih Muslim that it was a full year. Al-Mawardi related from her a third opinion, that it was sixteen months, and he mentioned no other from her. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the period between the beginning of al-Muzzammil and its end was one year. He said: "As for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it was obligatory upon him." In one report from him there are two views: one, that it remained obligatory upon him until Allah took him; the second, that it was abrogated for him just as it was abrogated for his community. Regarding the period of its obligation until it was abrogated there are two views: one, that it is the period set for his community in the two previous opinions, namely Ibn 'Abbas's saying "a year" and 'A'isha's saying "sixteen months." The second: that it was ten years, until it was lightened for him through abrogation, an increase in the obligation so that he would be distinguished by the performance of the message. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. I say: This contradicts what al-Tha'labi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as mentioned earlier, so consider it carefully. Further explanation of this issue will come at the end of the surah, Allah willing.

The eighth issue: His saying, "And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation" (al-Muzzammil 4), meaning: do not hasten in reciting the Qur'an, but recite it slowly and clearly, reflecting on its meanings. Al-Dahhak said: "Recite it letter by letter." Mujahid said: "The people most beloved to Allah in recitation are those who understand it best." Tartil means arranging, ordering, and good arrangement. From it comes the phrase "a thaghr ratal" and "ratal," with the 'ayn vowelled with a kasra or a fatha, meaning when the teeth are well arranged. Its explanation has already been given in the introduction of this book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 17.]

It is narrated by al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a man who was reciting a verse and weeping, and he said: "Did you not hear the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation'? This is tartil." 'Alqama heard a man reciting beautifully and said: "He has indeed recited the Qur'an in measured manner; may my father and mother be ransomed for him." Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: "Reflect upon the subtleties of His address, compel yourself to act upon its rulings, your heart to understand its meanings, and your inner self to turn towards it."

'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the Qur'an reciter will be brought, and he will be made to stand at the first step of Paradise, and it will be said to him: 'Recite, ascend, and recite in measured manner as you used to recite in the world, for your station will be at the last verse you recite.'" Abu Dawud recorded it, and it has been mentioned previously at the beginning of the book. [Editor's note in source: see vol. 1, p. 8.]

Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to prolong his voice in recitation, stretching the vowels.

God Almighty says: ﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a weighty word﴾. This is connected to what was made obligatory concerning the night prayer. That is, through the obligation of the night prayer, We will cast upon you a weighty word whose burden is heavy, because the night is for sleep. Whoever is commanded to stand in prayer for most of it can only manage this with a severe weight upon the self and a struggle against Satan, so it is a matter that is heavy upon the servant.

It has also been said: "Indeed, We will reveal to you the Qur'an, and it is a weighty word, the practice of whose laws is heavy." Qatadah said: "By Allah, its obligations and its limits are weighty." Mujahid said: "Its lawful and its unlawful." Al-Hasan said: "Acting upon it." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "Weighty in its promise and its threat, and in the lawful and the unlawful." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Weighty upon the hypocrites." It has also been said: "Weighty upon the disbelievers, because of the argument it makes against them, the clarification of their misguidance, the reviling of their gods, and the exposure of what the People of the Book had distorted." Al-Suddi said: "Weighty in the sense of noble, derived from the saying: 'So-and-so is heavy upon me,' meaning he is honoured by me." Al-Farra' said: "Weighty and dignified, not light and worthless, because it is the speech of our Lord." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "Weighty, which none can bear except a heart supported by success and a soul adorned with monotheism." Ibn Zayd said: "By Allah, it is weighty and blessed, just as it was weighty in this world, it will be weighty in the Balance on the Day of Resurrection." It has also been said: "Weighty" means "firm," like the firmness of a heavy object in its place, and its meaning is that its miraculous nature is firm, and its inimitability will never cease.

It has also been said: the weighty word is the Qur'an itself, as came in a report that the Prophet (ﷺ), when revelation came to him while he was on his she-camel, she would lay her jirān (i.e., her chest) on the ground, and she could not move until [[i.e., the revelation.]] was lifted from him. In the Muwatta' (the collection of hadith compiled by Imam Malik) and elsewhere, it is reported that he, peace be upon him, was asked: "How does revelation come to you?" He said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the hardest on me, and it departs from me after I have retained what was said. And sometimes the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says." 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I have seen revelation descend upon him on a very cold day, and it departs from him while his forehead is pouring with sweat."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is preferable, because it is the reality. And He has said: ﴿He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]." And he, peace be upon him, said: "I have been sent with the upright and tolerant monotheism (al-Hanifiyyah al-Samhah)."

It has also been said: the "word" in this surah is the statement "There is no god but Allah," for in a report: "It is light upon the tongue and heavy in the Balance," related by al-Qushayri.

There are five issues in this verse.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾. The scholars said: "Nashi'at al-layl" means its times and its hours, because its times arise one after another. It is said: "nasha'a al-shay'u yansha'u" when it begins and comes one thing after another; so it is "nashi'" and Allah "anshaahu" so it "nasha'a." From this comes "nasha'at al-sahabah" when the cloud began, and Allah "anshaahaa." So "nashi'ah" is a feminine active form from "nasha'at tansha'u fahiya nashi'ah." From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or is one who is brought up in ornaments, and in dispute is not clear?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 18]. The meaning is: indeed, the hours of the rising night; he suffices with the description instead of the noun. The feminine form refers to the word "sa'ah" (hour), because every hour comes into being. It was also said: "al-nashi'ah" is a verbal noun meaning "qiyam al-layl" (standing in the night) [[An addition required by the wording, and it is so in the books of tafsir.]], like "al-khati'ah" and "al-kadhibah," meaning: indeed, the rising of the night is more firm in treading. It was also said: indeed, "nashi'at al-layl" is "qiyam al-layl." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The Abyssinians say 'nasha'a,' meaning he stood," so perhaps he meant that the word is Arabic [[In a, h, l: (strange). See vol. 1, p. 68 and what follows.]], but it is widespread in the speech of the Abyssinians and prevalent among them. Otherwise there is nothing in the Qur'an that is not in the language of the Arabs. This has already been explained fully in the introduction of the book.

The second: In this verse, Allah, exalted is He, makes clear the virtue of night prayer over day prayer, and that increasing in night prayer through recitation in it as much as possible is greater for the reward and more attracting of reward. The scholars differed concerning what is meant by "nashi'at al-layl." 'Ubadah said: "ashaddu wat'an" means more energetic for the one who prays and lighter, and firmer for recitation.

"Pouring out, when the swift ones upon weariness
Raise the dust with the hard, rolled ground."

Al-kadid: a rough place. Al-markal: that which is struck with feet. "Lighten (fasakh) the worry upon you, and know that
When the Merciful decrees a thing, it is coming to pass."

Al-Asma'i: it is said "sabbakha Allahu 'anka al-humma," meaning He lightened it. "Sabakha al-harr" means it subsided and eased. "Al-tasbikh" is deep sleep. "They released them, scattering the dust as
One scatters the carded pieces of cotton from the bowstring-ginned mass."

Tha'lab said: "al-sabkh" with a kha' is trembling and agitation, and "al-sabkh" also means calm, and from it is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Fever is from the heat of Hell, so cool it with water," meaning calm it. Abu 'Amr said: "al-sabkh" means sleep and free time. I say: on this basis it would be one of the words with opposite meanings, and it would have the meaning of "al-sabh," with an unpointed ha'.

There are three issues in this verse.

Sahl said: "Recite *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* at the beginning of your prayer; the blessing of its recitation will bring you to your Lord and cut you off from everything else" [[In manuscripts a, h, z, t: "tahwāhu" (what you desire)]]. It was also said: remember the name of your Lord in His promise and His threat, so that you devote yourself to obeying Him and turn away from disobeying Him. Al-Kalbi said: "Pray to your Lord," meaning during the day.

I say: This is good, for when He mentioned the night, He mentioned the day, since it is its counterpart. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other for whoever wishes to remember or to be grateful﴾ [al-Furqan 25:62], as has already been explained.

The second is His saying, ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾. *Tabattul* (wholehearted devotion, cutting oneself off) means dedicating oneself to the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that is, sever yourself to His worship and do not associate anything with Him. It is said: "I cut the thing" (*battaltu al-shay'*), meaning I severed it. From this come the expressions: "He divorced her *battatan batlatan*" and "This is an irrevocable, *batlah* charity," meaning it is a severed gift, its ownership cut off from its giver entirely. From this comes Mary, *al-Batul* (the virgin), because she devoted herself to Allah the Exalted. A monk is called *mutabattil* because he cuts himself off from people and devotes himself alone to worship. The poet said:

*She lights up the darkness at nightfall, as if she were*
*the lamp of a monk who has devoted himself, at his evening vigil.*

[[The verse is from the Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays. Its meaning: when she smiles at night you see the brightness and radiance of her teeth; when she appears in darkness her face shines until it overcomes the darkness of the night. "Mumsa rahib" means his evening time.]]

There is a hadith forbidding *tabattul*, which means withdrawing from people and from congregations. It was said that its original meaning among the Arabs is solitude; this was said by Ibn Arafa. The first meaning is stronger because of what we have mentioned. It is asked: why did He say *tabtil* (complete devotion) and not *tabattul*? It is answered: because the meaning of *tabattul* is "to cut oneself off," so it was brought in that form to match its meaning, in observance of the rhythm of the verse endings (*fawasil*).

The third is what has already passed in *al-Ma'idah* in the commentary on His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:87]. This was disliked for one who devotes himself and cuts himself off, following the way of monasticism, while what suffices him is available. Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for today, when the covenants of people have become corrupt, their trustworthiness has diminished, and the unlawful has taken control over worldly wealth (*hutam al-dunya*, meaning all the wealth of this world that perishes and does not last), then seclusion is better than mixing with people, and being alone is better than marrying. But the meaning of the verse is: sever yourself from idols and statues and from the worship of anything other than Allah. Likewise Mujahid said: its meaning is: make worship sincerely for Him, and he did not intend *tabattul*. So *tabattul* is commanded in the Qur'an and forbidden in the Sunnah. The object of the command is not the same as the object of the prohibition, so they do not contradict each other. The Prophet was sent only to explain to people what was revealed to them. The *tabattul* that is commanded is severing oneself to Allah through sincere worship, as He the Exalted says: ﴿They were commanded only to worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:5]. The *tabattul* that is forbidden is following the path of the Christians in abandoning marriage and practicing asceticism in monasteries. However, when times become corrupt, the best wealth of a Muslim will be a flock of sheep, which he follows to the mountain peaks and the places where rain falls, fleeing with his religion from trials.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 73, verses 9–11:

Allah's statement: ﴿The Lord of the East and the West﴾. The people of the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Hafs read "Rabbu" with a raised vowel (ḍamma), as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "there is no god but Him." It is also said that it is by supposing an implied "huwa" (He). The rest read "Rabbi" with a lowered vowel (kasra), as an epithet (na't) of the Lord, Exalted is He, in His statement: "And mention the name of your Lord" (Rabbi al-mashriq). Whoever knows that He is the Lord of the easts and the wests, his work and his hope are cut off from everything else and attached to Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 73, verses 15–19:

God's words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger﴾. He means the Prophet (ﷺ), whom He sent to Quraysh, ﴿as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾, who was Moses, ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾, meaning he denied him and did not believe. Muqatil said: He mentioned Moses and Pharaoh because the people of Makkah looked down on Muhammad (ﷺ) and treated him lightly, since he was born among them, just as Pharaoh looked down on Moses, since Moses had been raised and grew up among them, as God said: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]. Al-Mahdawi said: The alif and lam were added to "al-rasul" (the messenger) because it had already been mentioned, and for this reason it is chosen at the beginning of letters, "Peace be upon you," and at their end, "Peace be upon you."

(Wabilan) means heavy and severe. "Darb wabil" and "ʿadhab wabil" mean severe. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. From this comes "matar wabil," meaning heavy rain, as said by al-Akhfash. Al-Zajjaj said: It means heavy and harsh. From this, rain is called wabil. It was also said: destructive, and the meaning is that We punished him with a harsh punishment [[The addition is from the marginal notes of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi, and its text is his wording.]]. He said:

"You devoured your sons like the lizard devours, until you found the bitter taste of the harmful pasture."

"Fulan istawbala kadha" means he did not approve of its outcome. "Ma' wabil" means unwholesome and hard to digest. "Kala' mustawbal" and "ta'am wabil wa mustawbal" mean food that is not digestible and not wholesome. Zuhayr said:

"They divided their fates among themselves, then they came back to a pasture unwholesome and noxious."

Al-Khansa' said:

"Bajila devoured, on the day it met the horsemen of Malik, a devouring that was harmful."

Al-Wabil also means a large staff. He said:

"Were it that in my right hand is its rein, and in my other hand is a staff I fear."

Likewise, "al-mawbal" with a kasra on the ba' is also used, and "al-mu'bilah" means a bundle of firewood. Likewise "al-wabil." Tarafah said:

"The beloved of an old man like a staff, quarrelsome [[Yalanddid: strong in dispute. The first half of the line is: "So she passed like a she-ass with a pregnant belly, a splendid one..."]]."

God's words: ﴿then how will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, on a Day that will make the children grey-haired?﴾ This is rebuke and reproach, meaning: how will you protect yourselves from the punishment if you disbelieve? There is an inversion in it, meaning: how will you guard yourselves against a day that makes the children grey-haired, if you disbelieve? This is also the reading of ʿAbd Allah and ʿAtiyyah. Al-Hasan said: meaning, by which prayer will you guard yourselves against the punishment? By which fasting will you guard yourselves against the punishment? There is an implied element in it, meaning: how will you guard yourselves against the punishment of a day? Qatadah said: By God, whoever disbelieves in God will not be protected on that day by anything. "Yawman" is the object of "tattaqun" according to this reading, and not an adverbial of time.
