**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 73, verse 20 (part 1 of 3)**

In this verse there are thirteen issues (masa'il).

**First:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] ...﴾. This verse explains His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or subtract from it a little, or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:2–4], as has already been mentioned. It abrogates (naskh) the obligation of the night prayer, as has already been mentioned. "Taqum" means "tusalli" (you pray), and "adna" means "aqall" (less).

Ibn al-Samaiqa, Abu Haywa, and Hisham, from the people of Syria, read "thuluthay" with a sukun on the lam. The majority (al-'amma) read "nisfahu" and "thuluthahu" in the genitive case (bi-l-khafd), in coordination with "thuluthay," meaning: you stand for less than two-thirds of the night and for its half and its third. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, as in His saying: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, and ﴿How can they stand for half of it or a third of it, when they cannot keep count of it?﴾ 

Ibn Kathir and the Kufans read "nisfahu wa thuluthahu" in the accusative case, in coordination with "adna," the meaning being: you stand for less than two-thirds of the night, and you stand for its half and its third. Al-Farra' said: "This is closer to the correct reading, because He said 'less than two-thirds,' and then mentioned the very quantity of less, not less than less."

Al-Qushayri said: According to this reading, it is possible that they used to observe a third and a half, since standing for that amount was light for them, and they used to exceed it, and in exceeding it is the attainment of the purpose. As for two-thirds, standing for that was heavy on them, so they did not attain it and fell short of it. It is also possible that they were commanded to stand for half the night, and were given leniency to add or subtract, so they would go up in addition to nearly two-thirds, and down in the half to a third. It is also possible that half was prescribed for them and reduced to a third, while the addition went up to two-thirds, and among them were those who fulfilled that, and among them those who left it, until it was abrogated for them. 

Some people said: Allah only obligated them a quarter, and they used to reduce from the quarter. This view is arbitrary (tahakkum).

**Second:** His saying: ﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾, meaning: He knows the exact measures of the night and the day as they truly are, while you know them through estimation (taharri) and effort (ijtihad), in which error may occur.

﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾, meaning: you would not be able to know its realities and to fulfil it. It was said: meaning, you would not be able to stand for the night prayer. The first is more correct, for the night prayer was never obligated in its entirety.

Muqatil [in manuscript Z: "al-Naqqash"] and others said: When ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or subtract from it a little, or add to it﴾ was revealed, this was hard for them. A man would not know when half the night was, or when a third of it was, so he would stand until morning, fearing that he might err. Their feet swelled and their faces paled. So Allah had mercy on them and lightened [the burden] for them, and He said: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾. "Anna" here is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna" (indeed), meaning: He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, because if you added to it, it would be heavy upon you, and you would need to impose what is not an obligation; and if you reduced it, that would be hard upon you.

**Third:** His saying: ﴿So He turned to you﴾, meaning: He returned to you with pardon. This indicates that some of them had neglected some of what they were commanded. It was also said: meaning: He relented toward you from the obligation of standing, since you were unable. The origin of repentance (tawbah) is return, as has already been mentioned, so the meaning is: He returned to you from burden to ease, and from hardship to facility. They were only commanded to keep track of the times by way of estimation (taharri), so that estimation was lightened for them.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾ is that He creates them as measured, like His saying: ﴿And He created everything and measured it precisely﴾. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The measure of creation is not connected to a ruling; rather, Allah ties to it what He wills of the duties of obligation (wazaif al-taklif).

**Fourth:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾. On this there are two views. The first is that what is meant is recitation itself, i.e., recite in your night prayer what is light for you. Al-Suddi said: one hundred verses. Al-Hasan said: whoever recites one hundred verses in a night, the Qur'an will not argue against him. Ka'b said: whoever recites one hundred verses in a night is recorded among the devout (al-qanitin). Sa'id said: fifty verses.

I say: the saying of Ka'b is more correct, due to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever stands in prayer with ten verses is not recorded among the heedless; whoever stands with one hundred verses is recorded among the devout; and whoever stands with one thousand verses is recorded among the (

Al-Tabari... no. Here is the translation:

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi transmitted it in his Musnad, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr. We have mentioned it in the introduction to this book [[see vol. 1, p. 9]], and praise be to Allah.

The second opinion: "So recite what is easy of it" means: pray what is easy for you. Prayer is called Qur'an, as in His saying, exalted is He: "and the recitation of dawn" (Qur'an al-Fajr), meaning the dawn prayer (salat al-fajr). Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the most sound opinion, because it reports about the prayer, and the statement returns to it.

I say: the first opinion is more sound, since it takes the address according to the apparent wording, whereas the second opinion is figurative, for it is the naming of a thing by part of its actions.

Fifth: Some scholars said: the saying of Allah, "So recite what is easy of it," abrogated (naskh) the night prayer (qiyam al-layl) and half of it, and the reduction from half and the addition to it. Then the saying of Allah, "So recite what is easy of it," admits of two meanings. One is that it is a second obligation, because another obligation was removed by it. The other is that it is an abrogated obligation, removed by something else, just as something else had removed it, and this is based on His saying: "And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you; it may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station" [al-Isra': 79]. So His saying, "And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you" [al-Isra': 79], admits the meaning: he should pray, beyond what was obligatory for him, whatever is easy of it. Al-Shafi'i said: it was therefore necessary to seek evidence from the Sunnah for one of the two meanings, and we found that the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indicates that there is no obligatory prayer except the five.

Sixth: Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the well-known view is that the abrogation of the night prayer applied to the community, while the obligation remained for the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: the fixed measure was abrogated, but the basic obligation remained, as in His saying: "Then what is easy of the sacrificial animal" [al-Baqarah: 196]. The sacrificial animal is indispensable, and likewise the night prayer was not dispensable, but its amount was left to the choice of the one praying. On this basis, some people said: the obligation of night prayer with a little remains, and this is the view of al-Hasan. Others said: it was abrogated completely, so the night prayer is not obligatory at all, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Perhaps the obligation that remained for the Prophet (ﷺ) is this, namely standing in prayer at night, with its amount left to his choice. Since it has been established that standing is not obligatory, His saying, "So recite what is easy of it," means: recite if that is easy for you, and pray if you wish. Some people went further and held that complete abrogation was also established for the Prophet (ﷺ), so the night prayer was never obligatory for him. And His saying, "a supererogatory act for you" [al-Isra': 79], is taken in its literal sense of voluntary worship. As for the one who says that the measure was abrogated while the basic obligation of standing in the night remained and was then abrogated, this second abrogation occurred through the explanation of the prayer times, as in His saying: "Establish prayer at the decline of the sun" [al-Isra': 78], and His saying: "So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning" [al-Rum: 17], and what is in the report that additions to the five prayers are voluntary. It was also said: the abrogation occurred by His saying, "And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you" [al-Isra': 79], and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the community, just as the obligation of prayer, though addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in His saying, "O you who are wrapped up! Stand [in prayer] through the night" [al-Muzzammil: 1-2], was general to him and to others. It has also been said that the obligation from Allah continued until after the Hijrah and was abrogated in Medina, based on His saying: "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others fighting in the cause of Allah" [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Fighting was prescribed only in Medina. On this view, the explanation of the prayer times took place in Mecca, and the standing in prayer at night was abrogated by His saying: "And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you" [al-Isra': 79]. Ibn Abbas said: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, the saying of Allah, "Indeed your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] [nearly] two-thirds of the night" [al-Muzzammil: 20], abrogated the obligation of night prayer.

Seventh: His saying, "He knows that there will be among you those who are ill" [al-Muzzammil: 20], up to the end of the verse. Allah, glorified is He, explained the reason for the lightening of the night standing. Among people there are the sick, for whom standing at night is difficult, and for whom missing prayer is difficult. The traveler in trade may not be able to stand at night, and likewise the one who fights in jihad. So Allah lightened it for all of them because of these people. In "an-sa-yakoonu" [anna sa-yakunu], the "anna" is the lightened form of the heavy one, meaning: He knows that it will be.

Eighth: In this verse, Allah equated the rank of those who strive in jihad with the rank of those who earn lawful wealth to support themselves and their dependents, and to do good and be generous. This is evidence that earning wealth is equal to jihad, because He joined it with jihad in the cause of Allah. Ibrahim reported from Alqamah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one brings food from one land to another and sells it at the price of its day except that his station with Allah is the station of the martyrs." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "and others traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others fighting in the cause of Allah." Ibn Mas'ud said: whoever brings something to a city of the Muslim cities, patiently and seeking reward, and sells it at the price of its day, has the station of the martyrs with Allah. Then he recited, "and others traveling through the land" [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Ibn Umar said: there is no death Allah has created that I would die after death in the cause of Allah more beloved to me than dying between the two sides of my saddle, seeking Allah's bounty while traveling through the land. Tawus said: one who strives for the widow and the poor is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah. It is reported from one of the early generations (al-salaf) that he was in Wasit, and he dispatched a boat of wheat to Basra, and he wrote to his agent: "Sell the food on the day it enters Basra, and do not delay it until tomorrow." It happened that there was a rise in prices. The merchants said to the agent: "If you delay it a week, you will profit many times over." So he delayed it a week and profited many times over. He wrote to his employer about this, and the owner of the food wrote back to him: "O man! We had been content with a small profit together with the soundness of our religion, and you have committed a wrong against us. When this letter of mine reaches you, take the money and give it in charity to the poor of Basra, and I wish that I could be saved from hoarding, neither in my favor nor against me." It is also reported that a young man from the people of Mecca used to stay constantly at the mosque. Ibn Umar missed him, so he walked to his house. His mother said: "He is attending to his food, which he is selling." He met him and said to him: "O my son! What is it to you with food? Why not camels, why not cattle, why not sheep! The owner of food loves scarcity, while the owner of livestock loves rain."

Ninth: His saying, "So recite what is easy of it" [al-Muzzammil: 20], means: pray as much as possible. Allah made obligatory from the night prayer what is easy, and then that was abrogated by the obligation of the five prayers, as already mentioned. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people said that the obligation of standing at night was prescribed in two units (rak'ah) from this verse. This was said by al-Bukhari and others, and he compiled a chapter in which he mentioned the hadith: "Satan ties three knots on the back of the head [qafiyat al-ra's, the back part, or some say its middle] of one of you when he sleeps, striking on each knot: 'You have a long night, so sleep.' If he wakes and remembers Allah, one knot is undone. If he performs ablution, another is undone. If he prays, all his knots are undone, and he becomes energetic and good of spirit; otherwise he becomes evil of spirit and lazy." He also mentioned the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub from the Prophet (ﷺ) about the dream: "As for the one whose head is crushed with a stone, he takes the Qur'an and rejects it [yarfudu-hu, he abandons it], and sleeps through the obligatory prayer." And the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: a man who sleeps the whole night was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "That is a man in whose ears Satan has urinated." Ibn al-'Arabi said: these are hadiths requiring that the general term "prayer" be understood as the obligatory prayer. The general is therefore understood in light of the specific, since it allows for that, and the claim of those who specified it as night standing falls away. In the Sahih, and the wording is that of al-Bukhari: Abdullah ibn Amr said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Abdullah, do not be like so-and-so, who used to stand in prayer at night, then he abandoned standing at night." Had it been obligatory, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have approved of it, nor would he have reported such a thing about him; rather he would have censured him in the strongest terms. Also in the Sahih, from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: in the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), when a man saw a dream, he would relate it to the Prophet (ﷺ). I was a young, unmarried boy, and I used to sleep in the mosque during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I saw in a dream as if two angels took me and brought me to the Fire. It was enclosed like the enclosure of a well, and it had two horns, and in it were people whom I recognized. I began to say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the Fire." He said: "Another angel met us and said to me: 'You have nothing to fear.'" I related it to Hafsah, and Hafsah related it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "What a fine man Abdullah is, if only he would pray at night." After that he would sleep only a little at night. So if abandoning standing were a sin, the angel would not have said to him: "You have nothing to fear." And Allah knows best.

Tenth: Since it has been established that night standing is not obligatory, and that His saying, "So recite what is easy of the Qur'an," and "So recite what is easy of it," is to be taken in its apparent sense of recitation in prayer, the scholars differed about the amount one must recite in prayer. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah) cannot be replaced, nor can one suffice with part of it. Abu Hanifah set the amount at one verse from whatever part of the Qur'an. It is also reported from him: three verses, because that is the shortest surah. Al-Mawardi mentioned the first view, and Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned the second. The correct view is what Malik and al-Shafi'i held, as we explained in the commentary on Surah al-Fatihah at the beginning of this book, and praise be to Allah. It was also said: the intended meaning is the recitation of the Qur'an outside prayer. Al-Mawardi said: on this view, the absolute command is understood either as obligation or as recommendation short of obligation. This is the view of most scholars, because if it were obligatory to recite, it would be obligatory to memorize it. The second view: it is understood as obligatory, so that through his recitation he may witness its inimitability and the proofs of monotheism and the sending of messengers in it. Yet if he recites it and recognizes its inimitability and the proofs of monotheism in it, he is not obliged to memorize it, because memorizing the Qur'an is among the recommended acts of devotion, not the obligatory ones. Regarding the amount of recitation contained in this command, there are five views: the first is the entire Qur'an, because Allah made it easy for His servants, said by al-Dahhak. The second is one third of the Qur'an, reported by Juwaybir. The third is two hundred verses, said by al-Suddi. The fourth is one hundred verses, said by Ibn Abbas. The fifth is three verses, like the shortest surah, said by Abu Khalid al-Kinani.

Eleventh: His saying, "And establish the prayer" [al-Muzzammil: 20], meaning the obligatory prayer, which is the five prayers at their appointed times.

(And establish the zakah) the obligatory zakah on your wealth, so said Ikrimah and Qatadah. Al-Harith al-Ukli said: it is the zakat al-fitr (charity of breaking the fast), because the zakah on wealth was made obligatory after this. It was also said: it is voluntary charity. And it was said: it is every act of goodness. Ibn Abbas said: obedience to Allah and sincerity toward Him.

The twelfth issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾. The goodly loan is that which is intended for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, purely from lawful wealth. Its explanation has already passed in Surah "al-Hadid" [[See vol. 17, p. 252]]. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the goodly loan is spending on one's family. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: it is spending in the way of Allah.

The thirteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted: (And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah) [[See vol. 2, p. 73.]]. It is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he prepared a dish of hays, meaning dates with milk, and a poor man came to him, so he took it and gave it to him. Some of those present said: this poor man does not know what this is! Umar said: But the Lord of the poor man knows what it is. It seems he interpreted: "whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, it is better (khayran)," meaning better than what you left behind and kept back, and than stinginess and negligence.

(And greater in reward) Abu Hurayrah said: it is Paradise. It may also mean greater in reward, since He gives ten times for one good deed. The words khayran and a'zama are in the accusative as the second object of (tajidūhu). According to the Basrans, huwa is a separator (fasl), and according to the Kufans it is a pronoun of emphasis (imad), having no place in the i'rab. And ajran is a specifying noun (tamyiz).

(And seek forgiveness from Allah): i.e., ask Him for forgiveness for your sins. (Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving) toward what preceded repentance, (Most Merciful) toward you after it, so said Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The surah ends. [[In manuscript L: "The surah ends, and praise be to Allah."]]
